```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse   = TRUE,
  comment    = "#>",
  fig.width  = 7,
  fig.height = 4.5
)
options(scipen = 999)
```

```{r setup}
library(PRA)

# 10,000 iterations locally; fewer on CRAN so the vignette builds quickly.
n_sims <- if (nzchar(Sys.getenv("NOT_CRAN"))) 10000L else 1000L
n_lev  <- if (nzchar(Sys.getenv("NOT_CRAN"))) 5000L else 500L
```

`mcs()` treats a project as the **sum** of its task durations. That is exact
for a single chain of tasks, but real schedules have parallel paths,
overlapping work and shared crews. Where paths merge, the finish is set by
whichever path runs longest in that iteration. This *merge bias* makes the
expected finish later than any single path suggests, even when every
estimate is symmetric. A shared resource can also hold an activity back
after its predecessors are done.

PRA's schedule functions analyze the network itself:

| Function | Does |
|---|---|
| `project_schedule()` | Validates activities, links, duration distributions, resources, assignments and risk events |
| `cpm()` | Deterministic critical path method, optionally resource-leveled |
| `sra()` | Monte Carlo schedule risk analysis: reruns CPM in every iteration |

All three results have `print()`, `summary()` and `plot()` methods.

# Why not just add up durations?

Two 10-week activities run in parallel, each with a symmetric triangular
estimate of 8 to 12 weeks. On paper the project takes 10 weeks.

```{r merge-bias}
parallel <- project_schedule(
  activities = data.frame(id = c("Start", "X", "Y", "Finish"),
                          duration = c(0, 10, 10, 0)),
  links = data.frame(source = c("Start", "Start", "X", "Y"),
                     target = c("X", "Y", "Finish", "Finish")),
  duration_dists = list(
    X = list(type = "triangular", a = 8, b = 10, c = 12),
    Y = list(type = "triangular", a = 8, b = 10, c = 12)
  ),
  time_unit = "weeks"
)
set.seed(1)
par_risk <- sra(parallel, n_sims)
par_risk$prob_deterministic
par_risk$total_mean
```

The 10-week plan has only about a one-in-four chance of being met. A
task-sum model of either path would put it at one in two.

# The building project schedule

`building_project` includes a resource-loaded schedule for the six work
packages of a mid-rise building, in weeks:

```{r data}
bp <- building_project
bp$schedule_activities
bp$schedule_links
```

The envelope (T4) starts 8 weeks into the structural frame (start-to-start)
and finishes at least 2 weeks after it (finish-to-finish). MEP rough-in
starts 4 weeks into the envelope. Fit-out follows envelope dry-in and must
finish at least 4 weeks after MEP. Fit-out has no duration of its own: it is
24 crew-weeks of work by two finishing crews, so its duration depends on crew
productivity.

```{r resources}
bp$schedule_resources
bp$schedule_assignments
```

A single tower crane serves the foundations, frame and envelope. Each
resource's `rate` is its cost per unit per week, and `fixed_cost` carries
materials and lump sums.

```{r build}
proj <- project_schedule(
  activities         = bp$schedule_activities,
  links              = bp$schedule_links,
  duration_dists     = bp$duration_dists,
  resources          = bp$schedule_resources,
  productivity_dists = bp$productivity_dists,
  assignments        = bp$schedule_assignments,
  risks              = bp$risk_register,
  cor_mat            = bp$cor_mat[1:5, 1:5],
  start_date         = bp$start_date,
  time_unit          = "weeks"
)
proj
```

```{r network-plot, fig.cap = "Activity-on-node network. Red marks the deterministic critical path; edge labels give non-FS link types and lags."}
plot(proj)
```

# Deterministic critical path

```{r cpm}
plan <- cpm(proj)
plan
```

The forward pass gives each activity's early start: the latest of zero and
the constraint of each incoming link. FS gives predecessor finish + lag, SS
gives predecessor start + lag, FF gives predecessor finish + lag − duration,
and SF gives predecessor start + lag − duration. The backward pass mirrors
this from the project finish. *Total float* is late start minus early start.
*Free float* is the slip an activity can absorb before it delays any
successor.

```{r cpm-gantt, fig.cap = "Deterministic schedule. Grey bars show total float; the dashed line is the project finish."}
plot(plan)
```

## Resource leveling

The baseline overlaps the envelope with the frame, but both need the one
crane. `level = TRUE` schedules activities with a serial
schedule-generation scheme. It repeatedly takes the eligible activity with
the smallest late start and places it at the earliest time that satisfies its
links and keeps every resource within capacity for the activity's whole
duration.

```{r leveled}
leveled <- cpm(proj, level = TRUE)
leveled$finish - plan$finish
```

```{r leveled-gantt, fig.cap = "Resource-leveled schedule: the envelope waits for the crane."}
plot(leveled)
```

The crane conflict costs eight weeks. Under leveling, criticality comes from
the *driving path*. It traces back from the finish through binding links and
through resource hand-offs, because float has no meaning once resources move
dates.

# Schedule risk analysis

`sra()` samples durations, crew productivity and risk events, then
reschedules the network in every iteration. Here the crane constraint is
respected throughout:

```{r sra}
set.seed(2027)
risk <- sra(proj, num_sims = n_lev, level = TRUE)
risk
```

```{r finish-plots, fig.show = "hold", fig.cap = "Project finish: histogram and cumulative probability."}
plot(risk, type = "finish")
plot(risk, type = "cdf")
```

The leveled deterministic plan sits low on the cumulative curve. The gap
reflects correlated, right-skewed durations, uncertain crew productivity and
the two risk events. Contingency follows directly:

```{r contingency}
contingency(risk, phigh = 0.80, pbase = 0.50)
```

## Which activities drive the finish?

```{r activity-stats}
summary(risk)$activities
```

* The **criticality index** is the share of iterations in which the activity
  is critical.
* **Sensitivity** is the Spearman rank correlation between the activity's
  duration and the project finish.
* The **cruciality index** is criticality × sensitivity (Williams, 1992). It
  ranks activities by how much they actually move the finish. An activity
  that is always critical but never varies has a cruciality of zero.
* The **schedule sensitivity index** (SSI) is criticality × sd(duration) /
  sd(finish) (PMI, 2009).

```{r gantt, fig.cap = "Deterministic bars shaded by criticality index, with P10-P90 finish whiskers and P50 ticks."}
plot(risk, type = "gantt")
```

```{r tornado, fig.cap = "Activities ranked by cruciality."}
plot(risk, type = "tornado")
```

```{r crit-network, fig.cap = "Network shaded by criticality index."}
plot(risk, type = "network")
```

## Risk events

Each risk in the register occurs independently in each iteration with its
stated probability. When it occurs, a sampled delay is added to every
activity it affects, and its cost impact is added to project cost.

```{r risks}
risk$risk_stats
```

`finish_impact` is the mean finish in iterations where the risk occurred
minus the mean where it did not. `cost_impact` is the same difference in
total cost, so it includes the extra resource cost of the delay as well as
the risk's own cost. Rank risk responses by these impacts:

```{r risk-tornado, fig.cap = "Risk events ranked by mean finish impact."}
plot(risk, type = "tornado", metric = "risk")
```

## Cost and resources over time

Each activity's cost is its resource cost (`units × rate × duration`) plus
fixed cost plus its share of risk costs. It is spread over the activity's
dates and accumulated into a cost S-curve band:

```{r cost, fig.cap = "Cumulative cost: P50 line and P10-P90 band."}
plot(risk, type = "cost")
risk$cost_percentiles
```

Resource usage is summarized the same way. With leveling, no iteration
exceeds capacity:

```{r resource-usage, fig.height = 6, fig.cap = "Resource usage against capacity."}
plot(risk, type = "resources")
```

## What does the crane constraint cost?

Comparing the leveled analysis with an unconstrained one prices the
resource constraint in probabilistic terms:

```{r compare}
set.seed(2027)
free <- sra(proj, num_sims = n_sims)
rbind(
  unconstrained = free$percentiles,
  leveled       = risk$percentiles
)
```

With a single crane, the P80 finish moves from
`r round(free$percentiles[["80%"]], 1)` to
`r round(risk$percentiles[["80%"]], 1)` weeks. That is the figure to weigh
against the cost of a second crane.

# Notes and limitations

* Time is in abstract units from a common start. A `start_date` with
  `time_unit = "days"` or `"weeks"` labels plot axes in calendar dates.
  Working calendars and date constraints are not modelled.
* Duration correlation uses the same Gaussian copula as `mcs()`, and every
  marginal distribution is preserved. Productivity draws and risk events are
  independent.
* Sampled durations are truncated at zero.
* Leveling uses one priority rule. It is a realistic heuristic, not an
  optimizer, and it schedules each iteration separately, so it is slower than
  unleveled analysis on large networks.

scheduling. *Proceedings of the Eastern Joint Computer Conference*, 160–173.

Kolisch, R. (1996). Serial and parallel resource-constrained project
scheduling methods revisited: Theory and computation. *European Journal of
Operational Research*, 90(2), 320–333.

Project Management Institute (2009). *Practice Standard for Project Risk
Management*. PMI.

Williams, T. M. (1992). Criticality in stochastic networks. *Journal of the
Operational Research Society*, 43(4), 353–357.
